coverage: This is a closed-universe matter. Each step forbids any authority, facts, or data beyond the listed uploads and requires citations by exact document name with page and paragraph, so I judged criteria first against the uploads. I compared real law only where a criterion's correctness depends on it, or where the uploads themselves point to it. I read the pinned original PDFs (rendered page images) for the comparator memorandum and the Award to confirm the extractions; they match. Read in full: the assignment-2 instruction (with stipulated facts (a)-(c)), the accumulated assignment-1 prompt, all five uploads (the Douglas opinion in full, focusing on printed pp. 331-35; DCMR § 1606), and all 12 criteria including three penalties. Law checked this session (targeted passage searches of CourtListener opinion text, not full reads): the Douglas parallel citation (5 M.S.P.R. 280 = 5 MSPB 313), confirmed by Tartaglia v. Dep't of Veterans Affairs, 858 F.3d 1405 (Fed. Cir. 2017) (citing '5 MSPB 313, 331-32, 5 M.S.P.R. 280'), and the location of the 'not to be evaluated mechanistically' passage at 5 M.S.P.R. 306, confirmed by McNab v. Dep't of the Army, 2014 MSPB 79. The uploaded copy matches that passage at its printed p. 333. Minor point not flagged: criterion 6 attributes 'balancing' to DCMR § 1606.2, but in the upload § 1606.2 requires managers to 'be prepared to demonstrate that the following factors were considered,' and the balancing duty is in § 1606.3 ('All of these factors shall be considered and balanced'). A lenient judge will credit a response that cites either; the impact is 4 points at most. Criteria reviewed with no defect established (9 of 12): 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 8, 10, 11, 12.

findings.title: The Award's 'Douglas, 5 M.S.P.R. at 306' is a correct cite; the upload is paginated in the parallel MSPB reporter
findings.explanation: Criterion 9 (+30 of 88) requires the response to identify that the Award's citation to 'Douglas ..., 5 M.S.P.R. 280, 306' 'does not correspond to any page of the uploaded Douglas opinion,' because the upload is 'paginated 313 to 346.' Douglas has two reporter citations: 5 M.S.P.R. 280 and 5 MSPB 313. The upload carries the MSPB pagination (first page 313), and the Award's pincite is the correct M.S.P.R. page for the 'tolerable limits of reasonableness' discussion, which appears at printed p. 333 of the upload. The instructions themselves designate the document as 'Douglas v. Veterans Administration, 5 M.S.P.R. 280 (1981),' so the uploaded document's own label signals parallel pagination. The rubric is internally inconsistent: criterion 1 of this assignment, and the sources for assignment-3 criterion 3 and assignment-5 criteria 4, 7, and 8, cite 'Douglas ..., 5 M.S.P.R. 280, 305-06,' the same M.S.P.R. pages this item says do not exist. A careful lawyer would say the Award's citation is accurate and give the corresponding upload pages (MSPB 332-33). That response fails 30 points, while a response that calls a correct citation an error passes. The item tests a misreading of reporter pagination, not citation diligence.

findings.title: 'No uploaded authority requires MPD to prove comparability' sits uneasily with Douglas's burden-of-persuasion holding
findings.explanation: Criterion 4 (+26 of 88) requires the response to identify 'that no uploaded authority requires MPD to prove the comparability of its comparator cases.' The prompt asks which party 'bore the burden of production and persuasion on the comparator evidence at each stage.' The uploaded Douglas opinion answers that 'the ultimate burden is upon the agency to persuade ... of the appropriateness of the penalty' and that 'selection of an appropriate penalty is a distinct element of the agency's decision, and therefore properly within its burden of persuasion.' A prima facie case suffices only 'when no issue has been raised concerning the penalty'; once the employee 'challenges the severity of the penalty,' the agency must present further evidence. Here the stipulated arbitral issue was 'is the penalty of termination appropriate?' DCMR § 1606.2 also requires managers to 'be prepared to demonstrate' that consistency (factor f) was considered. A careful associate could conclude that, once the penalty was contested, MPD bore the burden of persuasion on its factor-six consistency rationale, so the arbitrator's 'failed to carry its burden' language has some footing in Douglas, even if his 'prove comparability' framing overstated it given Douglas's warning against 'mathematical rigidity.' The criterion fails that answer. A narrower reading ('no authority makes strict comparability a threshold element') is defensible, so the item is arguable rather than problematic.

findings.title: The -18 'initial showing' penalty can hit MPD's strongest position as grounded in the uploaded Douglas
findings.explanation: Penalty misfire: criterion 5 deducts 18 points for stating 'that the employee must make an initial showing of disparate treatment before the agency bears a comparator burden,' on the theory that this rule 'relies on authority outside the uploaded materials.' The upload contains a version of the rule. Douglas says a prima facie case 'will normally suffice' when 'no issue has been raised concerning the penalty,' and the agency must present 'further evidence' only when the employee challenges it. Stipulated fact (b) says Braddock never alleged disparate treatment before the hearing, and the prompt asks for the legal consequence of that failure and 'the strongest position MPD can take.' The natural MPD position is that, under Douglas's burden-shifting structure, MPD's prima facie comparator showing sufficed because disparate treatment was never raised. A response that states this, citing Douglas, risks the penalty. It is arguable because Braddock did contest the penalty generally, and Douglas's 'challenges the severity of the penalty' is broader than a specific disparate-treatment showing.
